keyVerseText: And it came to pass, when their hearts were merry, that they said, Call for Samson, that he may make us sport. And they called for Samson out of the prison house; and he made them sport: and they set him between the pillars. them: Heb. before them
rootMeaning: The Hebrew verb שָׂחַק (sâchaq) is a primitive root that fundamentally conveys the act of laughing or playing. Its core sense encompasses both joyful laughter and mockery, reflecting a range of emotional expressions from delight to derision. This duality in meaning highlights that the root captures not just the physical act of laughter but also the social and emotional contexts in which laughter occurs, including playful interaction and scornful ridicule.
usageInScripture: Across its 36 occurrences, שָׂחַק appears with a spectrum of meanings centered on laughter and play, as seen in translations like 'played,' 'shall laugh,' and 'make merry.' The word is used both for innocent, joyful play and for laughter with contempt or mockery, indicating its flexible application in Scripture. This range reveals that שָׂחַק is not limited to a single emotional tone but rather conveys the complexity of human and even divine responses expressed through laughter and sport.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding שָׂחַק enriches our grasp of Scripture by revealing how laughter and play are woven into the human experience as ordained by God, encompassing both joy and judgment. The presence of mockery and derision within its semantic field reminds believers of the reality of scorn faced by the righteous, as well as God's sovereign use of laughter in His dealings with the world. This verb invites reflection on the balance between rejoicing in God's goodness and recognizing the seriousness of sin and opposition. Ultimately, it points to the hope that God, who 'laughs' in triumph, sustains His people amid trials and mockery.
keyVerseReflection: Judges 16:25 states, 'And it came to pass, when their hearts were merry, that they said, Call for Samson, that he may make us sport.' Here, שָׂחַק conveys the idea of making sport or playing before an audience, underscoring the scene's grim irony where Samson is brought out to entertain those who oppose him. The word deepens the narrative by emphasizing the mixture of merriment and mockery, revealing how laughter can serve as both amusement and a means of humiliation within God's providential story.
